newsitem.title: FRANCE: French trucker dies in accident amid protests.
newsitem.headline: French trucker dies in accident amid protests.

text.p: A striking French truck driver was crushed to death by a lorry he tried to stop at a blockade on a day of protests to accuse bosses of failing to honour a deal reached after a 12-day stoppage in 1996.
Didier Pinson, 41, a member of the independent Force Ouvriere (FO) union, slipped under the wheels of the slow-moving truck at Saint-Vincent-de-Paul near Bordeaux in the southwest.
Witnesses said he had clambered onto the running-board and pounded the windscreen with his fists, cracking it to try to persuade the driver to stop.
A state prosecutor said the death appeared to be an accident and opened an inquiry for manslaughter.
FO asked the government to step in and quickly arrange talks to restore calm and end the conflict which is taking place during the campaign for a parliamentary election on May 25/June 1.

Truckers set up two blockades at fuel depots near Bordeaux as part of a day of action around France by the drivers, who say employers have failed to honour a government-backed pact last year including higher pay and retirement at 55 instead of 60.

The national road information centre said that blockades were focused around Bordeaux, where Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor, and in the north. Blockades led to long tailbacks near the Channel port of Calais.
The National Road Haulage Federation, which groups employers, said the stoppage had no impact on its business.

Stoppages also disrupted public transport in many provincial cities, with bus and tram drivers pushing for concessions on retirement. The protests are a reminder of union power in the run-up to a parliamentary election on May 25/June 1.
Four truckers' unions called the one-day protest after accusing employers of backing out of the deal that ended the 12-day truck strike across France last November.

Employers agreed to retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers with 25 years' service, sick pay, travel expenses, union rights and a ban on Sunday driving. They also agreed a special bonus payment of 3,000 francs ($600).
Talks about implementing the deal broke down when unions and haulage bosses failed to meet a March 31 deadline.
"Out of 3,776 drivers who filled the conditions (for retirement at 55), only 350 will be able to benefit," complained Roger Poletti, head of the transport branch of the FO union.

Parked lorries straddled three roads and prevented oil company tankers reaching two key depots at Brassens, on the outskirts of Bordeaux. But passenger cars and other light vehicles were allowed through.
The strikes were called by the FO and the Communist-led CGT union, which together spearheaded a 24-day public sector stoppage in 1995 that virtually paralysed France.
The pro-Socialist CFDT union called a strike for public transport, urging early retirement at 55.
In the north-eastern city of Lille, buses and trams were paralysed and rubbish collections were disrupted. The city's two underground railway lines were unaffected.
In Montpellier in the south, public transport was cut by half. About 100 drivers from the Languedoc area marched through the city in protest.
In Clermont-Ferrand, about 95 percent of public transport unionists were on strike. No buses ran in Dijon in the east. Transport was unaffected in Paris and Lyon, France's biggest cities.
